nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the baroque lyric and the prose of the arts
literary_identity: Poet and critic of the arts; the youngest Sitwell and the prose poet of the baroque.
biography: Born Sacheverell Sitwell at Scarborough on 15 November 1897, the youngest of the three poetic Sitwells; he served briefly in the war and published The People's Palace (1918) before turning to the prose of the arts in The Spanish Scene (1927) and to the baroque lyric of The Dance of the Quick and the Dead (1935). His books on architecture, ballet, painting and gardens made him the critic of the arts for half a century; he died at Salisbury on 9 July 1988.
literary_profile: Sacheverell Sitwell is the prose poet of the baroque and the critic of the arts: his lyric of the 1920s and 1930s carried the Sitwell sound-pattern into the long poem of the palace and the fountain, and his books on Spain, the baroque, ballet and the garden created the English prose of the arts as a genre of its own.
stylistic_characteristics: The long, loaded, alliterative line of the baroque lyric; the poem as a palace, a fountain or a firework; the prose of the connoisseur, describing painting, ballet and architecture in the cadence of the poem; the catalogue as a form of pleasure; the image of the quick and the dead in the same stanza.
intellectual_concerns: The baroque and the rococo as the arts of surprise; Spain, Italy and the south as the theatre of the eye; ballet, painting and architecture as the subjects of the prose poem; the garden and the flower as the memory of a civilisation; the family and the quarrel of the three poets.
historical_significance: Sacheverell Sitwell is the prose poet of the baroque and the critic of the arts: his lyric of the palace and the fountain carried the Sitwell sound into the long poem, and his books on Spain, the baroque, ballet and the garden created the English prose of the arts as a genre of its own.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the first theorist of imagism and the translator of the French poets
literary_identity: Poet, translator and critic; the author of the 1913 manifesto 'Imagisme' in Poetry magazine.
biography: Born Frank Stuart Flint in London on 19 November 1885; he worked as a clerk and a journalist, founded the Poets' Club and the Secession Club, and with Ezra Pound and T. E. Hulme shaped the doctrine that his essay 'Imagisme' (Poetry, March 1913) published to the world. His own verse - In the Net of the Stars (1909), Cadences (1915), Otherworld (1920) - and his translations of the French symbolists carried the new manner into English; he died in London on 28 February 1960.
literary_profile: F. S. Flint is the first theorist of imagism: his essay of March 1913 stated the three rules - direct treatment, no superfluous word, the cadence of the musical phrase - that the movement took as its manifesto, and his translations of the French symbolists gave the English lyric its new model. His own verse is the record of the doctrine's first practice.
stylistic_characteristics: The short unrhymed cadence of the French vers libre; the image stated without comment; the translation that carries the cadence rather than the rhyme; the lyric of the window, the street and the evening; the prose of the manifesto, exact and polemical.
intellectual_concerns: The image and the rule of the direct treatment; French poetry and the vers libriste school; the little magazine as the institution of the new verse; the clerk's London and the evening street; the quarrel with Pound over the ownership of imagism.
historical_significance: F. S. Flint is the first theorist of imagism: his essay of March 1913 stated the three rules the movement took as its manifesto, and his translations of the French symbolists gave the English lyric its new model of the unrhymed cadence and the stated image.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the peasant drama of the Abbey and the reteller of the Irish and Greek tales
literary_identity: Poet, playwright and folk-teller; a founder of the Abbey peasant play and the reteller of The King of Ireland's Son.
biography: Born Padraic Colum at Longford on 8 December 1881; he was a founder of the Abbey Theatre's peasant drama with The Land (1905) and The Fiddler's House (1907), a poet of the Irish lyric in Wild Earth (1907), and the reteller of the Irish and Greek tales in The King of Ireland's Son (1916) and The Children's Homer. He moved to the United States in 1914 and taught at Columbia; he died at Enfield, Massachusetts, on 11 January 1972.
literary_profile: Padraic Colum is a founder of the Abbey peasant play and the great reteller of the tale: The Land and The Fiddler's House put the Irish small farmer on the stage beside Synge's, and The King of Ireland's Son and The Children's Homer made the Irish and the Greek stories the common property of English-speaking childhood. His lyric of the Irish road and the emigrant ship is among the best of the revival.
stylistic_characteristics: The spoken Irish idiom carried into English dialogue; the peasant scene built on the land question and the emigrant ship; the tale retold in the plain narrative sentence of the storyteller; the lyric of the road, the fair and the leaving; the comic exchange set against the elegiac set speech.
intellectual_concerns: The land and the small farmer; emigration and the ship; the Irish tale and the Greek tale as the inheritance of childhood; the Abbey and the peasant play; exile in America and the remembered Ireland.
historical_significance: Padraic Colum is a founder of the Abbey peasant play and the great reteller of the tale: The Land and The Fiddler's House put the Irish small farmer on the stage, and The King of Ireland's Son and The Children's Homer made the Irish and Greek stories the property of English-speaking childhood.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Georgian lyric of the country and the critic of the modern poets
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and critic; the Georgian lyricist of the country and the author of Eight for Immortality.
biography: Born Richard Thomas Church at Battersea on 26 March 1893; he worked as a civil servant until 1933, publishing verse from 1917 in the Clarion and the periodicals, and made his name with the lyrics of A Glance Backward (1930), News from the Mountain (1932) and The Solitary Man (1941), with the novels Oliver's Daughter (1930) and High Summer (1931) beside them. His criticism of the modern poets in Eight for Immortality (1941) and his three volumes of autobiography, from Over the Bridge (1955), closed the career; he died on 4 March 1972.
literary_profile: Richard Church is the last and one of the finest of the Georgian lyricists: his lyrics of the country, the mountain and the solitary man carried the plain observed lyric through the modernist decades, his novels of the English village held the realist manner of the 1930s, and Eight for Immortality is a key document of the reception of the modern poets by their Georgian contemporaries.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain observed lyric of the country and the season; the narrative poem of the village; the novel of the English village in the realist manner; the criticism that reads the modern poets through the Georgian ear; the autobiography of the enchanted ordinary.
intellectual_concerns: The country and the vanishing rural world; the solitary man and the life of the lyric; the English village and its church; the reception of the modern poets by their contemporaries; the enchantment of the ordinary as the subject of autobiography.
historical_significance: Richard Church is the last and one of the finest of the Georgian lyricists: his lyrics of the country and the solitary man carried the plain observed lyric through the modernist decades, and Eight for Immortality is a key document of the reception of the modern poets by their Georgian contemporaries.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the founder of the Gaelic League and the playwright of the Irish-language Abbey drama
literary_identity: Scholar, playwright and founder of the Gaelic League; 'An Craoibhín Aoibhinn', the first President of Ireland.
biography: Born Douglas James Hyde at Castlerea, County Roscommon, on 17 January 1860, the son of a Church of Ireland rector; he grew up among the Irish speakers of Frenchpark and founded the Gaelic League in 1893. His one-act plays in Irish - Casadh an tSugáin (The Twisting of the Rope, 1901), The Marriage, The Lost Saint - opened the Irish-language drama of the Abbey, and his Religious Songs of Connacht (1906) is the great collection of the Irish religious lyric. He was elected the first President of Ireland in 1938 and died in Dublin on 12 July 1949.
literary_profile: Douglas Hyde is the founder of the Gaelic League and the first playwright of the Irish-language theatre: The Twisting of the Rope, played at the Abbey in October 1901, was the first play in Irish seen on a Dublin stage, and his collections of the songs and religious lyrics of Connacht made the Irish-speaking west the source of the literary revival. As first President of Ireland he carried the revival into the state.
stylistic_characteristics: The spoken Irish of Connacht carried into English by the translation of Lady Gregory; the one-act play of the cottage and the road; the religious lyric and the charm collected from the mouth of the singer; the scholar's exactness in the collector's note; the gaiety of the Irish idiom in the comic exchange.
intellectual_concerns: The Irish language and the de-Anglicising of Ireland; the songs, prayers and charms of Connacht; the cottage play and the Abbey stage; the scholar as the collector of the living speech; the revival as the recovery of a language rather than of a politics.
historical_significance: Douglas Hyde is the founder of the Gaelic League and the first playwright of the Irish-language theatre: The Twisting of the Rope was the first play in Irish seen on a Dublin stage, and his collections of the songs of Connacht made the Irish-speaking west the source of the literary revival.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the founder of Practical Criticism and of the semantics of the poem
literary_identity: Critic and rhetorician; the author of Principles of Literary Criticism and Practical Criticism.
biography: Born Ivor Armstrong Richards at Sandgate, Kent, on 26 February 1893; he read philosophy and English at Cambridge and taught there from 1919, where the experiments of the classroom became Principles of Literary Criticism (1924), Science and Poetry (1926) and Practical Criticism (1929). Coleridge on Imagination (1934) and The Philosophy of Rhetoric (1936) carried the argument into the theory of metaphor; his later work on Basic English took him to China and Harvard, where he died on 7 September 1979.
literary_profile: I. A. Richards founded the modern discipline of practical criticism: the experiments of Principles of Literary Criticism and Practical Criticism made the reading of the poem, rather than its history, the object of the discipline, and gave the New Criticism of England and America its method and its vocabulary of the pseudo-statement, the impulse and the stock response.
stylistic_characteristics: The analytic prose of the psychologist of reading; the experiment and the protocol as the form of criticism; the definition and the distinction carried in the plain sentence; the rejection of the biographical and the historical in favour of the reading; the rhetoric of metaphor as the instrument of thought.
intellectual_concerns: The reading of the poem and the psychology of the reader; the pseudo-statement and the language of science; metaphor and the rhetoric of thought; Coleridge and the imagination; Basic English and the teaching of reading; the discipline of criticism as a science of the response.
historical_significance: I. A. Richards founded the modern discipline of practical criticism: Principles of Literary Criticism and Practical Criticism made the reading of the poem the object of the discipline and gave the New Criticism of England and America its method and its vocabulary.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the critic of ambiguity and the poet of the argumentative lyric
literary_identity: Critic and poet; the author of Seven Types of Ambiguity and Some Versions of Pastoral.
biography: Born William Empson at Yokefleet, Yorkshire, on 27 September 1906; he read mathematics and then English at Cambridge under I. A. Richards, and published Seven Types of Ambiguity in 1930, Some Versions of Pastoral in 1935 and his Poems in the same year. He taught in Japan and China through the war years and at Sheffield after them; his later criticism, from The Structure of Complex Words (1951), and his verse of the argumentative lyric made him the most original critic-poet of his generation. He died in London on 15 April 1984.
literary_profile: William Empson is the most original critic-poet of the English twentieth century: Seven Types of Ambiguity made the analysis of verbal ambiguity the instrument of the close reading that the century took as its method, Some Versions of Pastoral read the whole range of English literature as versions of the pastoral irony, and his poems are the argumentative lyric of the scientific intellect.
stylistic_characteristics: The close reading that unfolds every sense of the word; the argumentative lyric of the compressed syntax and the irony; the pastoral read as the social irony of the degree; the wit of the parenthesis and the aside; the prose that thinks in the sentence rather than in the paragraph.
intellectual_concerns: Ambiguity and the plurality of sense; the pastoral and the social irony; the complexity of the key word; Buddhism and the argument of the self; the mathematics and the poem; the quarrel with the doctrine of the unified response.
historical_significance: William Empson is the most original critic-poet of the English twentieth century: Seven Types of Ambiguity made verbal ambiguity the instrument of the close reading the century took as its method, Some Versions of Pastoral read English literature as versions of the pastoral irony, and his poems are the argumentative lyric of the scientific intellect.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the critic of the great tradition and the founder of the Cambridge school
literary_identity: Critic; the editor of Scrutiny and the author of The Great Tradition and Revaluation.
biography: Born Frank Raymond Leavis at Cambridge on 14 July 1895; he served in the war, took his degree at Cambridge and taught there, founding the journal Scrutiny in 1932. Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture (1930), New Bearings in English Poetry (1932) and Revaluation (1936) made him the most feared critic in England, and The Great Tradition (1948) fixed the canon of the English novel. He held the readership at Cambridge until 1962 and died there on 14 April 1978.
literary_profile: F. R. Leavis is the most influential English critic of the twentieth century: the polemic of Mass Civilisation and Minority Culture made the defence of the minority culture the task of criticism, New Bearings in English Poetry revalued the modern poets, Revaluation and The Great Tradition fixed the canons of the verse and the novel, and the school of Scrutiny trained the teachers of English for a generation.
stylistic_characteristics: The polemical sentence of the moral urgency; the quotation examined word by word in the argument; the verdict delivered as a definition; the rejection of the historical and the sociological in favour of the valuation; the canon as the instrument of the discipline.
intellectual_concerns: The minority culture against the mass civilisation; the valuation and the canon; the great tradition of the English novel from Austen to James; the revaluation of the English poets; the discipline of English as a defence of the civilisation; the war and the loss of the organic community.
